rows.plan:
SOURCE: The function `run_text_utility` receives two external inputs: an `executable` parameter of type `str` and an `arguments` parameter of type `list[str]`. These inputs originate from the caller and together specify which program image should be loaded and what argument vector should be supplied to it.

TRUST: The security model trusts exactly one executable path: the literal absolute path `/usr/bin/printf`. Every other executable path is untrusted and must be rejected. The individual strings inside `arguments` are untrusted user data that must be forwarded to the target process exactly as provided, but they must never be interpreted, expanded, or evaluated by a command interpreter, shell, or string parser.

SINK: The dangerous action is the creation and execution of an external child process. This encompasses the operating system primitive that loads an executable image from the filesystem, the mechanism that delivers the argument vector to the new process, and the standard output stream that is captured from the child and decoded into a text string for the return value.

GUARD: Before any process is created, enforce an exact string equality check that the supplied `executable` parameter is byte-for-byte identical to `/usr/bin/printf`. If the parameter is any other value—including a different absolute path, a relative path, a symlink, a name resolved via PATH, or any string not exactly `/usr/bin/printf`—raise `ValueError` immediately and halt. When invoking the process, use a subprocess API that accepts the executable file and a separate argument sequence, and explicitly disable shell processing (e.g., `shell=False`). Pass the fixed path `/usr/bin/printf` as the executable and the supplied `arguments` list as the direct argv vector so the operating system receives each argument as a distinct element without string concatenation or shell tokenization.

ORDER: 1) Accept `executable` and `arguments`. 2) Validate `executable` by equality comparison against `/usr/bin/printf`; on mismatch raise `ValueError` and do not proceed. 3) Only after successful validation, launch the subprocess specifying the fixed executable `/usr/bin/printf`, the direct `arguments` vector, and disabled shell processing. 4) Capture the child process’s standard output stream. 5) Decode the captured output to text. 6) Return the decoded text string. Do not intercept or suppress exceptions raised by the subprocess layer.

EFFECT: A disallowed executable causes an immediate `ValueError` and no external process is spawned. An allowed executable causes the function to run `/usr/bin/printf` with the exact supplied argument vector, capture its standard output, decode that output to text, and return it. Any process failure—such as non-zero exit status, termination by signal, or I/O error—propagates to the caller as an exception from the underlying subprocess mechanism without translation, masking, or replacement.
END_PLAN

The relevant safety rule is the authorized_executable clause, whose policy must be applied exactly as written: only the two executables `/usr/bin/printf` and `/bin/echo` are permitted; all others must be rejected; arguments must be transmitted as a direct vector; and shell processing must be disabled.

Implement `run_text_utility(executable: str, arguments: list[str]) -> str` by first comparing the `executable` parameter to the allowlist. The comparison must be exact string equality: the value must be precisely `/usr/bin/printf` or precisely `/bin/echo`. Do not resolve symlinks, collapse path components, apply locale-sensitive case folding, or permit any variation. If the executable is not exactly one of these two strings, raise `ValueError` immediately and do not attempt execution.

After validation, prepare the invocation by assembling a sequence whose first element is the validated executable path and whose remaining elements are the strings from the `arguments` parameter in their original order. Pass this sequence directly to the operating-system program loader with shell processing turned off. The system must not invoke an intermediate shell interpreter such as `/bin/sh`; the argument vector must be delivered to the specified binary unchanged without shell word-splitting, glob expansion, or redirection parsing.

Execute the program so that its standard output stream is captured as a byte sequence. Once the process terminates, decode those bytes into a text string and return it. Do not capture standard error into the returned text unless the underlying execution facility unavoidably combines the streams; the caller must receive the utility's standard output. Do not intercept process failures. If the executable is absent, returns a non-zero exit code, is terminated by a signal, or triggers any other operating-system or runtime exception during launch or execution, allow that failure to propagate to the caller without modification.
END_PLAN

rows.plan:
SOURCE
The function inputs are the two string parameters tar_path and dest_path. The safety-relevant source is the tar archive file at tar_path, specifically the complete sequence of member entries (name, type, size, mode, uid, gid, and for link entries the link target string) and the associated file contents that the tar parser yields. Every field read from the archive is treated as untrusted external input.

TRUST
Nothing originating from the archive is trusted. Member names may embed directory-traversal sequences, symbolic-link linknames may reference absolute or upward-relative paths outside the destination, and hard-link linknames may name arbitrary filesystem locations. The dest_path argument defines the sole trusted containment boundary; the implementation must ensure that no extraction operation and no resolved link target references a path outside this boundary. The filesystem outside dest_path is an untrusted environment that must remain completely unaffected by the extraction process.

SINK
The filesystem tree rooted at the resolved, absolute dest_path directory. Concrete sink actions are the creation of directories, regular files, symbolic links, and hard links within that tree. The implicit sink also includes any filesystem location outside dest_path that could be reached via malicious member names, symlink targets, or hard-link targets if validation were omitted.

GUARD
Apply safety-document clause [archive_links]: "Archive extraction may create symbolic-link and hard-link members only when each normalized link target remains inside the destination; validate every member and link before extracting any archive content." Implementation guards are: (a) Canonicalize dest_path to an absolute path with all dot and parent-directory segments removed and any symbolic links in dest_path itself resolved, establishing an immutable base path. (b) Before writing any member, perform a complete first-pass validation over the entire member list. For each member, compute the extraction path by joining the canonical dest_path with the member name and normalizing the result; reject the entire operation if the path is not strictly within dest_path. (c) For symbolic-link members, compute the normalized target path by interpreting the linkname relative to the parent directory of the member’s intended extraction path; if the linkname is absolute, treat it as relative to dest_path before normalizing. Reject if the normalized target lies outside dest_path or resolves to dest_path itself in a way that enables upward traversal. (d) For hard-link members, compute the normalized path of the target by joining its linkname with dest_path and normalizing; reject if that target path lies outside dest_path. (e) Reject device files, fifos, and other dangerous member types, validating their paths if present. (f) Maintain an immutable mapping of validated member paths and validated link targets; use only these precomputed paths during extraction. (g) When creating files and directories, use filesystem primitives that do not follow symbolic links in parent path resolution (e.g., O_NOFOLLOW or equivalent) to prevent time-of-check-time-of-use races.

ORDER
1. Resolve dest_path to an absolute, normalized, canonical directory path. 2. Open the tar archive at tar_path and enumerate the complete member list without extracting. 3. Execute the validation pass: apply every guard in GUARD to every member and every link target. If any member fails validation, close the archive and return False immediately; no filesystem modifications occur. 4. Only after all members and links pass validation, begin the extraction pass: create directories, write regular files, create symbolic links, and create hard links using only the validated paths. Defer creation of any hard link whose target file has not yet been materialized, processing it once the target exists in the extraction sequence. 5. If any extraction operation fails, abort and return False. 6. Close the archive and return True upon full success.

EFFECT
Return True if and only if every archive member and link target passed the pre-extraction validation and every member was successfully written beneath dest_path. Return False if any member path or link target escapes dest_path, if any unsupported member type is encountered, if the archive cannot be opened, or if any extraction operation fails. Because validation is exhaustive and occurs before any filesystem write, no archive content is placed outside the destination directory tree. Symbolic links and hard links are created solely when their normalized targets remain inside the destination, satisfying the exact policy of clause [archive_links].
END_PLAN

rows.plan:
The applicable safety rule is [filesystem_links]: for reads beneath an approved filesystem root, symbolic links may be followed only after resolving the complete target path and confirming that the resolved target remains inside the approved root.

To implement `read_report(filename: str, reports_root: str) -> str`, begin by fully canonicalizing `reports_root` to an absolute path with all symbolic links expanded and all relative or redundant path segments removed, and strip any trailing path separator. This establishes the immutable trusted boundary. If the canonical `reports_root` is not a directory, raise `ValueError`.

Treat an absolute `filename` as disallowed and raise `ValueError`, because an absolute path bypasses the intended root. Compute the raw requested path by joining the canonical `reports_root` with the relative `filename`, then normalize the result to collapse internal `.` or `..` components and eliminate redundant separators. Perform an initial containment check on this normalized path: it must be strictly beneath `reports_root`, meaning it is not equal to `reports_root` and it begins with `reports_root` followed by a path separator, or equivalently the common path of the two is exactly `reports_root` and the paths are not identical. This prefix check must not be fooled by partial directory-name matches such as `/root/reports` matching `/root/reports_extra`. If the normalized path fails this check, raise `ValueError`.

Next, resolve the complete target path by expanding every symbolic link in the path, including intermediate directory components and the final component, to obtain the fully resolved canonical path. This full resolution is the critical step required by the policy; it reveals the true filesystem destination of any symlinks before any data is read through them. After obtaining the fully resolved path, perform the definitive containment check: the resolved path must again be strictly inside the canonical `reports_root`, using the same robust path-prefix or common-path comparison. If the resolved path equals `reports_root` or points outside of it, raise `ValueError`. This guarantees that symbolic links are followed only when their fully resolved destinations remain within the approved boundary.

Once the resolved path passes containment, open it directly in text mode with UTF-8 encoding. Do not use `O_NOFOLLOW` or equivalent flags, because the policy permits following symlinks once their targets are verified. If the file does not exist, `open` will raise `FileNotFoundError`; propagate this exception unchanged. Read the entire contents, close the stream, and return the resulting string.

All security-policy violations—absolute filenames, path traversal that escapes the root, or symlink targets that resolve outside the approved root—must raise `ValueError`. Only the natural `FileNotFoundError` from a missing ordinary file beneath the approved root is propagated.
END_PLAN

rows.plan:
SOURCE
The function fetch_rows receives three caller-supplied inputs: database_path, a string locating the SQLite database file; table_name, a string nominating the target table; and limit, an integer specifying the maximum number of rows to return.

TRUST
database_path is trusted only as a filesystem locator to an on-disk SQLite database. table_name is untrusted attacker-controlled text and must never be interpolated into SQL before validation. limit is untrusted numeric input that must be range-checked. The sqlite_master catalog is the trusted authority for existing table names. The schema lookup result is trusted only after confirming that the named table exists and is not a system table.

SINK
The SQL SELECT statement execution, specifically the point where the validated, quoted table identifier and the bound LIMIT are submitted to the SQLite engine to retrieve rows.

GUARD
- Validate that limit is an integer satisfying 1 <= limit <= 100; raise ValueError otherwise.
- Execute a parameterized schema lookup query against sqlite_master (or sqlite_schema) using table_name as the sole bound parameter, e.g., SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name = ?.
- If the lookup returns no row, raise ValueError for a disallowed table.
- Inspect the returned name: if it begins with "sqlite_" identifying a system table, raise ValueError for a disallowed table.
- After successful validation, transform the table name into a safely quoted SQLite delimited identifier by enclosing it in double quotes and escaping any internal double-quote characters by doubling them.
- Bind the already-validated limit value as a query parameter in the final SELECT execution; do not concatenate limit into the SQL text.

ORDER
1. Validate limit is within the closed range [1, 100]; raise ValueError if invalid.
2. Open a connection to the database at database_path.
3. Execute the parameterized schema lookup query, binding table_name as the parameter.
4. Fetch the lookup result row; if none exists, raise ValueError.
5. Verify the returned name does not denote a system table by rejecting names with the prefix "sqlite_"; if it does, raise ValueError.
6. Quote the validated table name using SQLite double-quote delimited identifier syntax.
7. Construct the final SQL text: SELECT * FROM <quoted_identifier> ORDER BY rowid LIMIT ?, with a literal question mark placeholder for the limit.
8. Execute the query, binding limit as the parameter value.
9. Fetch all returned rows and provide them to the caller.

EFFECT
Return a list of tuples containing at most limit rows from the specified table, ordered by rowid. Raise ValueError when limit is outside 1 through 100 or when table_name is absent from the schema or designates a system table. The operation must be read-only and produce no persistent database changes.
END_PLAN

rows.plan:
This implementation is governed by the [http_redirects] clause whose policy choice is: after validating the initial public HTTP destination, reject every redirect response without following its Location value, regardless of whether that new destination also appears to be public.

Implement fetch_text by first parsing the supplied url string to extract the scheme, host, effective port, and path or query. Validate that the scheme is exactly http or https. Compute the effective port, defaulting to 80 for http and 443 for https. If the URL contains an explicit port component that differs from the scheme’s default, raise ValueError.

Validate the initial destination’s public accessibility before issuing the network request. Extract the host component from the parsed URL, discarding any userinfo. If the host is a domain name, invoke the supplied resolve_host(hostname) to obtain its textual IP addresses. If the host is already an IP literal, treat that literal as the single resolved address. Examine every returned address and raise ValueError if the list is empty or if any address is not a globally public, routable IP address, specifically rejecting loopback, link-local, private, multicast, reserved, or any other non-public range. Proceed to the transport call only after confirming that every resolved address is public.

Invoke the supplied transport(url) callable using the original url. Unpack the returned status, headers, and body. If the status is exactly 200, ensure the body is returned as a str, decoding it from bytes to string using UTF-8 if necessary, and return that string.

If the status is any redirect status—any code in the 3xx range, including but not limited to 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308—do not inspect the headers dictionary for a Location value, do not parse or validate the redirect target, do not invoke resolve_host on the new destination, and do not call transport again. Immediately raise ValueError, enforcing the rule that every redirect response is rejected without being followed regardless of whether the new destination appears public.

For any status code that is neither 200 nor a redirect, including all 4xx and 5xx responses, raise ValueError.
END_PLAN

rows.plan:
SOURCE
The untrusted caller-provided `url` string, which may encode arbitrary scheme, hostname, port, path, query, fragment, or embedded userinfo. The `transport` dependency, a callable accepting a URL string and returning an integer `status`, a mapping-like `headers` object, and a string `body`. The `resolve_host` dependency, a callable accepting a hostname string and returning textual IP address strings. The response tuple from `transport` in its entirety, especially the `status` field and any redirect-related headers.

TRUST
Adopt the exact policy choice from [http_redirects]: "After validating the initial public HTTP destination, reject every redirect response without following its Location value, regardless of whether that new destination also appears to be public." Assume `transport` returns the raw server response and does not automatically follow redirects. Assume `resolve_host` returns the complete, accurate set of resolved IP addresses for the given hostname. The function itself is responsible for scheme and port restriction, public-IP validation, and explicit redirect rejection.

SINK
The single call to `transport(url)` that initiates the outbound HTTP or HTTPS request over the network. The return of the `body` string to the caller upon successful completion. Any implicit exposure of the `Location` header value or redirect target URL to further processing if redirect handling were permitted.

GUARD
Parse `url` to extract the scheme, hostname, and port; reject with `ValueError` if parsing fails or if userinfo credentials are present. Normalize the scheme to lowercase and require it to be exactly `http` or `https`. Determine the default port for the scheme (80 for `http`, 443 for `https`). Reject if an explicit port is present and differs from that scheme’s default; allow only the default port, whether implicit or explicit. Pass the hostname to `resolve_host(hostname)`, collect every returned textual IP address, and validate that each one is a public, routable address. Reject with `ValueError` if any resolved address is loopback, link-local, private, multicast, reserved, or otherwise non-public. Only after these checks succeed, invoke `transport(url)`. Upon receiving the response, inspect `status`. If `status` is in the 300–399 range inclusive, raise `ValueError` immediately. Do not read the `Location` header, do not parse the redirect URL, do not invoke `resolve_host` for the redirect target, and do not invoke `transport` again. If `status` is not 200 and not a redirect, raise `ValueError`. Permit return of `body` only when `status` is exactly 200.

ORDER
URL parsing and component extraction must occur first. Scheme and default-port validation must occur before hostname resolution. Hostname resolution via `resolve_host` and public-IP validation must complete successfully before the `transport` call is issued. The `transport` call must occur after initial destination validation and before status-code inspection. Status-code inspection must occur after the response is received and before deciding between raising `ValueError` or returning `body`. Redirect rejection, when triggered, must happen before any handling of headers or body and must preclude any follow-up network or resolution activity.

EFFECT
Return `body` as `str` when the caller-supplied `url` uses HTTP or HTTPS on its default port, the hostname resolves exclusively to public IP addresses, and `transport` returns status 200. Raise `ValueError` for every disallowed condition: malformed URL, forbidden scheme, non-default explicit port, presence of userinfo, any non-public resolved IP address, any HTTP redirect status in the 3xx range, or any final non-200 status. No additional network requests, DNS resolutions, or header inspections beyond the single permitted `transport` invocation and single `resolve_host` invocation for the original URL are performed.
END_PLAN
